title: Science for a sustainable future

match.reason: No single bank point teaches this idea: the closest cards cover cost and uptake of practices or weighing effects of a mine, each only part of the brief, and the brief's link to sustainability and climate responses is not covered.

draft.title: Science for a sustainable future
card: Science can offer responses to issues such as climate change, water shortages and waste. These include new technologies, new methods and better information for decisions.
A response that works in a laboratory may not be taken up. Society also weighs its costs, its effects on people and the environment, and how easily it can be put in place.
Gains and losses are not shared evenly. A change can help one group and cost another, such as a new wind farm that gives cheap power to a city but changes the view for nearby residents.
So science can show what is possible and what is likely to happen. Whether to act is a choice made by communities, businesses and governments.
draft.remember: Science offers responses. Society takes them up depending on costs, effects and who gains or loses.

a.q: Scientists show that a new method can cut water use on farms. Which factor would most directly affect whether farmers take it up?
opts: The cost of setting it up compared with the savings
Whether the method was tested in a laboratory first
How many scientists have heard of the method
Whether the method uses a new scientific term
a.why: Uptake depends on costs, effects and who gains or loses, so the set-up cost matters to farmers. Testing in a laboratory is not the deciding factor, because a method that works there may still not be taken up.
a.clue: Think about what a farmer has to pay and what they get back.

b.q: A council in Gippsland is told that closing an old coal-fired power station would cut pollution. The station employs many local workers. What does this case show?
opts: A scientific response can help some groups and cost others
Scientific findings are wrong if some people lose out
Science alone decides what the council must do
The council should ignore the pollution evidence
b.why: Cutting pollution is a gain, but local workers may lose their jobs, so gains and losses are uneven. That does not make the evidence wrong, because science shows what is likely to happen while society decides what to do.
b.clue: Ask who gains and who loses.

a.best: The cost of setting it up compared with the savings

b.best: A scientific response can help some groups and cost others

problems.detail: The right option is the only one that is hedged ('can'), and it is slightly the longest. The three distractors are extreme absolute claims ('should ignore', 'are wrong if', 'alone decides ... must'), so a student could pick the answer without knowing the idea.

b.q: A council in Gippsland is told that closing an old coal-fired power station would cut pollution. The station employs many local workers. What does this case show?
opts: Closing it would help some groups and cost other groups
Closing it would affect every local group the same way
Lost jobs would make the pollution finding less reliable
The scientists who studied it would decide if it closes
